clue.text: Some banter if convict's accepted by Cambridge school

indicators.note: a thing accepted by something is taken in by it, so the school's name closes round the other letters

parts.note: the Perse School is a long-established independent school in Cambridge
a lag is slang for a convict, especially an old one; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: Someone remarks on a convict being admitted to a Cambridge school.
explanation.walkthrough: The Perse School is an old independent school in Cambridge; 'accepted by' has it take in the other two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Persiflage is light, mocking talk, a form of teasing banter.

clue.text: Cinderella's coach but no relation to the slipper

indicators.note: the word for relation is taken away, as if the coach came with no relatives

parts.note: in the fairy tale the fairy godmother turns a pumpkin into a coach
kin are relations, family members

explanation.surface: Cinderella's carriage has nothing to do with her glass shoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but no' removes KIN from PUMPKIN. In Britain a pump is a light slip-on shoe, like a dancing shoe.
explanation.definitionFit: A pump is a light, low-cut shoe, a slip-on for dancing.

clue.text: Waves for one's hair

definitions.meaning: long heavy waves rolling in from the sea
curlers wound into hair to set it

explanation.surface: Someone talks about the curls in their hair.
explanation.definitionFit: Big swells at sea are breakers; curlers used to set a hairdo bear the same name.

clue.text: Peculiarity of one form of dry cyanosis

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: a form of the words is their letters put in a new shape

explanation.surface: A doctor notes an odd feature of a type of dry blueness in the skin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'form of' rearranges DRY CYANOSIS after I for 'one'. Cyanosis is a bluish skin colour caused by lack of oxygen.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiosyncrasy is a quirk or habit peculiar to one person.

clue.text: Sugar-daddy sounds sweet

indicators.note: the two words for money and father, said together, are heard as the sweet

parts.note: lolly is British slang for money, as sugar can be, and pop is a word for daddy

explanation.surface: A rich older man's voice has a sweet tone.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'lolly' is slang for money, so 'sugar' becomes LOLLY and 'daddy' POP; said together they sound like the sweet on a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A lollipop is a boiled sweet on a stick, a confection for children.

clue.text: Writer's article supporting ego-development

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits beneath the other
the ego develops into a new form, its letters rearranged

parts.note: the is the definite article

explanation.surface: An author's essay boosts the growth of the self.
explanation.walkthrough: 'development' rearranges EGO into GOE, and 'supporting' puts THE below it in this down answer. The 's of 'Writer's' stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: Goethe was the great German poet and dramatist, author of Faust.

clue.text: Amphibian left when outnumbered?

indicators.note: out-numbered is read as numbered out of order, so the letters of the word for left are put in a new sequence

parts.note: went is the past tense of go, so left

explanation.surface: A small creature is abandoned once the others outnumber it.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'out-numbered', split to show the trick: WENT, for 'left', with its letters renumbered gives the creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A newt is a small tailed amphibian of ponds.

clue.text: Edward made her cross at Waltham

definitions.text: Edward made her cross at Waltham

parts.words: Edward made her cross at Waltham
parts.note: Edward I set up memorial crosses for his dead queen at each stop of her funeral procession, one at Waltham

explanation.surface: Edward annoyed a woman when they were in Waltham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made her cross' reads as annoyed her, but it is literal: Edward I built stone memorials for his queen, one at Waltham Cross in Hertfordshire, north of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward I's queen, of Castile, is commemorated by the stone crosses he built.

clue.text: First section in commonplace description of Gaul

indicators.note: the section goes in the other word, inside its letters

parts.note: trite means hackneyed, commonplace
part I is the first section of a work

explanation.surface: The opening part of a work holds a stock account of ancient France.
explanation.walkthrough: Caesar's Gallic War opens by saying that all Gaul is divided into three parts, so the opening section really does describe Gaul this way. PART I sits inside TRITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Caesar called Gaul divided into three parts, which is what three-part means.

clue.text: How adders proliferated, using logs

parts.note: adders reads as snakes breeding, but also as people who add; logarithms are the tables once used to do the next arithmetic operation up

explanation.surface: Snakes breed rapidly among a heap of logs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints snakes breeding under logs; the second reading is arithmetic, where people who add move on to the operation that logarithm tables were used for.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that proliferate increase greatly in number, and a sum done with log tables is a product.

clue.text: Head of village garlanded father of the tribe

annotationWithheld.why: Head of village garlanded father of the tribe (4): V placed inside LEI, but 'garlanded' must both supply LEI and signal the insertion, one word doing two jobs
annotationWithheld.clue: Head of village garlanded father of the tribe

clue.text: Peerie for instance to look into pigsty construction

indicators.note: the letters are put together into a new build

parts.note: to ogle is to look at, especially leeringly

explanation.surface: An archaeologist is sent to inspect a pigsty being built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'construction' rearranges TO, OGLE (for 'look') and PIGSTY. Flinders Petrie was a pioneering British archaeologist of Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Flinders Petrie was a famous British scholar of ancient Egypt and its pyramids.

clue.text: A refreshing change from the Orderly Room

definitions.text: A refreshing change from the Orderly Room

parts.words: A refreshing change from the Orderly Room
parts.note: a military unit's dining hall is where soldiers take refreshment away from the office, and an untidy state is the reverse of orderliness

explanation.surface: Soldiers leave the administrative office for a welcome break.
explanation.walkthrough: The Orderly Room is a regiment's administrative office; the dining room where service people eat is a break from it, and disorder is the opposite of a room kept orderly.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess is both a services dining hall and an untidy jumble, the opposite of order.

clue.text: Sacrifice needed to raise the wind

definitions.text: Sacrifice needed to raise the wind

parts.words: Sacrifice needed to raise the wind
parts.note: in Greek legend Agamemnon had to offer up his daughter so that winds would carry the fleet to Troy; to raise the wind is also slang for getting money

explanation.surface: Someone must give something up to raise funds.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'raise the wind' is old British slang for finding money, but here it is literal: the Greek fleet was becalmed at Aulis until Agamemnon offered up his daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the daughter of Agamemnon was offered to Artemis so that the becalmed fleet could sail.

clue.text: Teenager's misery during the climb

indicators.note: the misery happens during the climb, so it is placed within it

parts.note: an ascent is a climb
dole is an old word for grief or sorrow

explanation.surface: A young person feels wretched while climbing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' puts DOLE, an old poetic word for sorrow, inside ASCENT, after the A. The 's of 'Teenager's' stands for is.
explanation.definitionFit: An adolescent is a young person between childhood and adulthood.

clue.text: In sound I can create schism

indicators.note: the words before can be made into something new by rearranging their letters

explanation.surface: Someone claims that, being of sound mind, they are able to start a split.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can create' rearranges the letters of IN SOUND I. 'sound' looks like a call for a homophone, but it is only part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A schism is a split or breach within a group, a lack of unity.

clue.text: Petrol one needed in return journeys

indicators.note: the single letter is needed inside, so it is put within the other piece
on the return the word for journeys is read backwards

parts.note: trips are journeys
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Fuel is required for journeys there and back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' reads the word for journeys backwards, and 'needed in' sets the numeral inside. Petrol was once called motor spirit in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirit, or motor spirit, is a dated British name for petrol, the fuel for cars.

clue.text: Order it for a living-room or on the range

definitions.text: Order it for a living-room or on the range

parts.words: Order it for a living-room or on the range
parts.note: a command given to troops on a firing range, and also a grate burning unscreened in a lounge

explanation.surface: Someone asks for something to be ordered for the lounge or the kitchen stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'range' suggests a kitchen stove, but it is a firing range, where the words are a command; the same phrase names a hearth in a lounge.
explanation.definitionFit: The command to start shooting and an unguarded hearth in a room share the same words.

clue.text: Gloss lasts five years

definitions.meaning: a shine or sheen on a surface
a lustrum, also spelt this way, is a period of five years

explanation.surface: A shiny finish holds up for half a decade.
explanation.definitionFit: Lustre is a soft shine; the same word is an old form of lustrum, a span of a half-decade.

clue.text: Thus lawful to tout?

parts.note: so means thus, in this way
licit means permitted by law

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether touting for trade is therefore legal.
explanation.definitionFit: To solicit is to seek custom or tout for business.

clue.text: He's against work on repairing net round the pithead

indicators.note: the first group of pieces goes round the single letter, so it sits inside them

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
taken as written

indicators.note: repairing the net means fixing it into a new arrangement of its letters

parts.note: the head of the word pit is its first letter, P

explanation.surface: A man objects to working on mending a net near the top of a mine shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repairing' rearranges the letters of 'net', and 'round' has the first group enclose the head of 'pithead'; 'He's against' is the definition, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An opponent is someone who opposes or contends with you, a rival.

clue.text: Proclaim it's two' quarters over-weight

indicators.note: in a down clue the piece over another sits above it

parts.note: the compass quarters east and north give E and N
an ounce is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: Someone announces that two quarter-pounds are too heavy.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass points are the 'quarters': E and N. 'over' puts them above OUNCE in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To enounce is to state or pronounce formally, a rare word for announcing.

clue.text: Times so described (of course) by Charlie

definitions.text: Times so described (of course) by Charlie

parts.words: Times so described (of course) by Charlie
parts.note: Charlie Chaplin made a famous film about the industrial age called this kind of Times; and of course present-day times are described so

explanation.surface: A man named Charlie, naturally, gives his account of the newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Times' suggests this newspaper; it is the title of Chaplin's 1936 film about factory life, and any present-day times are of course described so too.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaplin's 1936 film is named for up-to-date times, the present age.

clue.text: In western bar leaders of the syndicate pinch a bit of silver

indicators.note: the leading letters go in the bar, inside its name

parts.note: a saloon is the bar of a Wild West town

indicators.note: leaders are the first letters of the following words

explanation.surface: In a cowboy bar the heads of a gang steal some silverware.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pinch' looks like the verb for steal, but it is the third word whose first letter is taken: T, S and P from 'the syndicate pinch' go inside SALOON.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny spoon for salt cellars, often made of silver, is a piece of table silver.

clue.text: Money once made some so bold

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Wealth was earned by a daring few.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' points to the run of letters inside 'so bold'.
explanation.definitionFit: An obol was a small silver coin of ancient Greece, a piece of currency no longer minted.

clue.text: Process appears right in a sense

indicators.note: the letter for right sits in the word for sense

parts.note: wit is good sense or intelligence

explanation.surface: A procedure seems correct in some respect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Process' is the legal sense: a court order served on someone. 'in' puts R inside WIT.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, process is the summons or court order served on a party.

clue.text: Do art work and so on with — end of brush

parts.note: etc. is the abbreviation of et cetera, and so on

indicators.note: the end of the word is its final letter

explanation.surface: An artist works with a brush, finishing with the tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of' takes the last letter of 'brush', H, which goes after ETC.
explanation.definitionFit: To etch is to make a design by cutting into metal with acid, a kind of printmaking craft.

clue.text: Wee French one getting sort of Reno divorce?

definitions.text: Wee French one getting sort of Reno divorce?

parts.note: petit is French for small
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: a sort of Reno is the city's name rearranged

explanation.surface: A small French person heads to Nevada for a quick divorce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges RENO into ONER. Reno, Nevada, was famous for quick divorces, and the whole clue describes who files for one.
explanation.definitionFit: In a divorce the person who files the suit is the party making a formal request to the court.

clue.text: Carry — your winnings after successful 29 hence?

definitions.meaning: the totalisator, the betting pool at a racecourse, pays out on a successful stake

explanation.surface: Someone must haul away the proceeds after a profitable punt.
explanation.walkthrough: 29 is INVESTMENT, so the second part is a bet that came off: the British racecourse betting pool pays winnings from it.
explanation.definitionFit: To tote is to lug a load; the same word is short for totalisator, the pool-betting system at races.

clue.text: May be stock form of warfare

definitions.meaning: shares or stock are a place for capital
the old military sense: surrounding a town to besiege it

explanation.surface: Shares might count as a kind of military campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock bought to make money is a holding of capital; besieging a fortress is the old military sense of the same word.
